 Rural Counties Urge Republicans to Negotiate SNAP Costs in Farm Bill
 The SNAP Fight That Hits Home
 Rural Counties Urge Republicans to Negotiate SNAP Costs in Farm Bill
11/13/2026 | 11:17 AM CST
 By 
 Jake Zajkowski
 ,
 DTN Ag Policy Editor
 Connect with Jake: 
 @jzajkow
 Steve Schmitt, a Meeker County, Minnesota, commissioner and local agriculturalist, speaks at a county fair. His county is among those facing higher costs as the federal government shifts more SNAP administrative expenses to states and local governments. (Photo courtesy of Steve Schmitt)
 WASHINGTON (DTN) --"Steve Schmitt knows the farm bill well. His father farmed, and he now transports grain, builds silos and sells seed in Meeker County, Minnesota.
 He has seen farm bills move quickly and others stall for years, as both a member of Farm Bureau and the county corn growers association."
 While passage of E15 and other provisions are priorities for him, at the top of his list, when it comes to his own tax dollars and those of the county he represents as a county commissioner, is the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP).
 Minnesota is one of 10 states where counties administer SNAP. Those counties now face higher administrative costs under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
 "Any cost shift to the state of Minnesota, in essence, is a cost shift to county government," he said. "We only have 24,000 residents, so these are real dollars, and as these shifts flow down to us."
 Beginning Oct. 1, 2026, the federal share of SNAP administrative costs fell from 50% to 25%, leaving states responsible for the remaining 75%, regardless of their payment error rates. Schmitt recognizes that some of the additional costs are already unavoidable.
 But Schmitt and thousands of county commissioners across the country are backing Senate Democrats' push for a two-year delay in the SNAP benefit cost-sharing requirements set to take effect in 2027. They want Senate Republicans to join the effort.
 Beginning Oct. 1, 2027, states with payment error rates of 6% or higher will begin paying a share of SNAP benefit costs. Their share will increase with their error rates.
 Meeker County has already calculated next year's cost. 
 The county expects to pay an additional $135,000 in SNAP administrative costs in 2027. In 2028, when the county absorbs a full year of the additional costs, that figure will reach $350,000. That increase alone represents more than three points on the county's property tax levy.
 "If they (Congress) see a county commissioner right now from the state of Minnesota, they pretty much know that it's about SNAP," he said.
 The additional costs are forcing Minnesota counties to make difficult budget decisions. This fall, counties are setting property tax levies at levels not seen since the 2008 financial crisis. About 85% of Meeker County's budget goes toward state-mandated spending, leaving just 15% for parks, libraries and other public services.
 "When the county government has to cut something, it cuts to the bone pretty quick. I mean, there's not a lot of fat on the bone, and to trim off," Schmitt said.
 He remembers discussing the food stamp program around the kitchen table with his father as a kid, including how the community used it and its connection to the farm bill.
 Today, those conversations center on what SNAP will cost his community and how many are being kicked off of it.
 The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities estimates 5.5 million fewer people will receive benefits because of eligibility changes since 2025. A USDA proposed rule released Monday would further reduce enrollment by eliminating broad-based categorical eligibility by 2029, potentially affecting another 6.3 million people.

 Schmitt did not expect the farm bill to create additional financial pressure for his county and harm his community.
 FARM BILL NEGOTIATIONS
 SNAP cost-sharing remains the farm bill's biggest sticking point. Nearly all other titles have been agreed upon, aside from several outstanding amendments.
 More Republicans are signaling openness to negotiations. Sens. Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, and Jim Justice, R-W.Va., have expressed interest in talks and a possible two-year delay in SNAP requirements.
 But Senate Agriculture Committee Chairman John Boozman, R-Ark., has not indicated a shift in the Republican position. He told DTN on Monday that "everything's on the table" and Republicans are negotiating in good faith.
 "I don't know if we can get it done or not, but it won't be for lack of trying, I think on both sides," he said.
 SHOULD THE STATE STEP IN?
 How much of the additional costs reach counties depends on each state's funding structure.
 Ten states administer SNAP at the county level: California, Colorado, Minnesota, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Virginia and Wisconsin.
 Several have provided one-time general fund appropriations in fiscal 2027 to help counties manage the administrative cost increases. Colorado, Wisconsin and New Jersey have allocated state funding to offset some of those costs, while New York and North Carolina have passed the increases entirely to counties.
 The New York State Association of Counties estimates counties will face an additional $168 million in annual expenses. That leaves local governments with few options: raise property taxes or reduce services. Some counties already operate under property tax caps, further limiting their options.
 "Counties see one-time state appropriations as a bridge, not a long-term solution," said Emma Conover, associate legislative director for human services and education at the National Association of Counties.
 She said one-time appropriations can help counties fund system upgrades to reduce payment error rates but do not cover recurring administrative expenses. A congressional delay would give counties more time to make those investments before also having to budget for the downstream benefit cost shift.
 Minnesota offers a middle-ground example.
 In May, state lawmakers approved a one-time allocation of $10.728 million to help counties cover additional SNAP administrative costs. However, that falls well short of the estimated $35 million in annual administrative expenses counties must absorb.
 Whether Minnesota provides additional assistance will depend on state finances and politics.
 "Unfortunately, in the state of Minnesota, the way the state budget shortfalls are looking over the next couple years, the next biennium, the state is not in a position to do that, and or probably doesn't really have a willingness because we're a DFL state," he said.
 States will have to continue exploring how to absorb the additional costs being shifted from Washington.
 MINNESOTA'S ERROR RATE
 Minnesota lawmakers approved some system modernization measures this year, but the changes will take time to implement and lower the state's payment error rate.
 Minnesota's current rate is hovering around 9%.
 The rate measures how accurately states determine household eligibility and benefit amounts, including both overpayments and underpayments.
 State agencies randomly select households for audits, examining eligibility and benefit calculations. In Minnesota, reviewers examine an average of 100 cases each month, while USDA reviews a subsample to validate the state's findings.
 County-level samples can be much smaller, sometimes involving just one file and other times five, Schmitt explained.
 That means a single overpayment in a one-file sample can produce a 100% county error rate. The statewide rate, however, is calculated using statistical analysis of the reviews rather than simply averaging county percentages.
 "If the state fails, we all fail. All 87 counties fail," he said.
 Larger counties, which serve more recipients and administer benefits on a much larger scale, face their own challenges in reducing error rates. Rural counties face different obstacles, including limited staffing and administrative capacity.
 "Counties believe that all states should benefit from a delay, and the same opportunity to improve systems, communicate eligibility changes, and ultimately lower payment error rates (PERs), especially in rural counties, where capacity and staffing can be limited, extra time to implement system changes can be critical in improving PERs and continuing to serve constituents," the National Association of Counties told DTN.
 "In two years, we should be able to be in a much better place than we are today," Schmitt said.
